candidates.attacker_control: The remote HTTP/2 peer controls the inbound control frames it sends (PING with attacker-chosen payloads, repeated SETTINGS, invalid stream references that trigger RST_STREAM) and controls whether it reads/consumes the server's responses (it can simply stop reading the TCP socket while continuing to send).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: (1) Checked that the class is truly unreachable: global searches for `Http2ControlFrameLimitEncoder`, `ControlFrameLimit`, `new Http2ControlFrameLimitEncoder`, and `maxOutstandingControlFrames` return only the class file itself and no wiring. (2) Checked other HTTP/2 DoS countermeasures: `Http2SettingsReceivedConsumer` exists and HPACK enforces `maxHeaderListSize`, but the lazy SETTINGS-ACK path is only used when `autoAckSettingsFrame` is explicitly disabled (default is true), so it does not bound the default path, and neither mechanism bounds PING ACKs/RST_STREAM. (3) Considered generic backpressure: channel writability watermarks do not gate these decoder-initiated control-frame writes, which are issued regardless of `isWritable()`. (4) Considered that the unused class could be a work-in-progress artifact rather than an intentional removal; either way the limiting code is absent from every runtime pipeline in this snapshot. (5) Could not execute code/tests or measure memory growth; impact is argued from source-level control flow only. (6) The exact historical fix commit/CVE identifier was not inspected (out of scope per instructions).
candidates.impact: Remote denial of service: unbounded server-side memory growth (outbound buffers plus per-frame promises/listeners) leading to GC pressure, heap exhaustion/OOM, or connection unavailability; also modest bandwidth amplification since small inbound control frames trigger outbound frames. The unused class's own Javadoc states it exists specifically to 'reduce the risk of DDOS' for this scenario.
candidates.prerequisites: A Netty endpoint using the stock HTTP/2 builders (`Http2FrameCodecBuilder`, `Http2MultiplexCodecBuilder`, or `Http2ConnectionHandlerBuilder`) without adding a custom limiting encoder, with default `autoAckPingFrame`/`autoAckSettingsFrame` values (both true in this snapshot), reachable by an untrusted HTTP/2 peer. Attacker needs to sustain a control-frame stream while refusing to read responses.
candidates.root_cause: codec-http2 ships a defensive wrapper, `Http2ControlFrameLimitEncoder`, that counts outstanding control frames it writes (PING ACK, SETTINGS ACK, RST_STREAM) and closes the connection with ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM once a configured maximum is reached (file lines 25-113, especially `handleOutstandingControlFrames`, lines 88-112). However, the class is dead code: a repository-wide text search finds no `new Http2ControlFrameLimitEncoder(...)` and no other reference to the type, so it is never wrapped around the connection encoder. All encoder construction paths install only `DefaultHttp2ConnectionEncoder` (optionally wrapped by `StreamBufferingEncoder`): `AbstractHttp2ConnectionHandlerBuilder.buildFromConnection` lines 470-486, `Http2FrameCodecBuilder.build` lines 179-186, `Http2MultiplexCodecBuilder.build` lines 205-212. No `maxOutstandingControlFrames` option exists on any builder either. At the same time `DefaultHttp2ConnectionDecoder` unconditionally writes a reply for attacker-triggered control frames: `onSettingsRead` writes a SETTINGS ACK whenever `settingsReceivedConsumer == null` (the default, since `autoAckSettingsFrame = true`, `AbstractHttp2ConnectionHandlerBuilder` line 108), lines 466-480; `onPingRead` writes a PING ACK whenever `autoAckPing` is true (default `autoAckPingFrame = true`, line 109), lines 482-489; RST_STREAM replies are also emitted by lifecycle error handling. Because these writes are never bounded or short-circuited, a peer that never reads the socket causes the control-frame responses and their channel promises/listeners to accumulate in Netty's outbound buffer until memory is exhausted.
candidates.title: HTTP/2 control-frame responses are unbounded: Http2ControlFrameLimitEncoder is never installed in any pipeline
candidates.trace: Peer sends PING frame -> DefaultHttp2FrameReader.readPingFrame -> DefaultHttp2ConnectionDecoder.onPingRead (autoAckPing default true, line 483-487) -> encoder.writePing(ack=true, ...) -> DefaultHttp2ConnectionEncoder.writePing -> DefaultHttp2FrameWriter writes an ACK frame whose promise completes only when the bytes are flushed. Peer does not read -> socket send buffer fills -> each additional ACK stays in ChannelOutboundBuffer with its promise/listener. The same unbounded path exists for SETTINGS (onSettingsRead -> writeSettingsAck, lines 466-474) and for RST_STREAM responses. The only intended guard, `Http2ControlFrameLimitEncoder` (which calls ctx.flush() once and then closes the channel at the limit, lines 88-112), is never constructed, so no count/limit/listener ever runs.
candidates.unverified: No runtime confirmation: I did not build or run Netty, send HTTP/2 frames, or measure buffer growth. The exact default limit intended by the author of `Http2ControlFrameLimitEncoder` and the exact upstream patch that wires it could not be inspected. It is possible some downstream application adds its own limiting encoder or disables auto-ack, which would mitigate the issue for those deployments. The relationship of this gap to a specific historical advisory/commit is inferred from the snapshot version (4.1.39.Final-SNAPSHOT) and the orphaned class, not proven.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-400 Uncontrolled Resource Consumption (missing HTTP/2 control-frame flood protection)

coverage_summary: Coverage was limited to the 1,988 repository-visible main source files reported by `get_source_scope` (no test sources are present in this snapshot); the P1 index reports all 1,988 files indexed with no hash mismatches or omissions, but index edges are syntactic navigation hints only and were verified against source text where used. I performed repository-wide literal searches (control-frame limit, auto-ack, CVE/TODO/comments, dangerous APIs) and targeted reading of codec-http2 (builders, decoder, frame codec, control-frame limit encoder, HPACK), codec-http (HttpObjectDecoder, HttpUtil paths, multipart classes), codec-haproxy, codec compression classes, buffer/common/transport spot checks, and the example/testsuite-supplemental modules by search only. I did not review every file, did not inspect the 11 native `.c` files in depth, and did not inspect build wiring beyond the POM/version evidence.

The P1 relation index is syntactic and incomplete for data flow/reachability; the 'unused class' conclusion was verified by repository-wide text search, but dynamic/reflective use cannot be fully excluded.

summary: Snapshot reviewed: Netty 4.1.39.Final-SNAPSHOT (main sources only, 1,988 files, no test sources). The strongest source-evidenced issue found is in codec-http2: the tree contains `Http2ControlFrameLimitEncoder`, a class whose own Javadoc says it exists to stop a peer that "will not consume our responses" from forcing a "massive amount of control frames" (DDOS), yet nothing in the repository ever constructs it and no builder exposes a limit. The default HTTP/2 pipelines auto-emit one control frame (PING ACK, SETTINGS ACK, RST_STREAM) per inbound control frame, so a remote peer that floods PING/SETTINGS/RST_STREAM and does not read responses accumulates unbounded outbound frames/promises in the channel outbound buffer (CWE-400 remote DoS). Other plausible historical weaknesses (HTTP/1 request smuggling in `HttpObjectDecoder`, HAProxy decoder bounds, Bzip2/multipart resource handling) were checked and are listed as rejected leads because they are not tied to any snapshot-specific artifact and, for the smuggling issues, the fix windows known for Netty do not match this snapshot's development version. No code was executed and no runtime behavior was confirmed.
